Mark 1: Early church writers such as Papias (around AD 120) say Mark wrote down Peter's preaching in Rome. Capernaum, Jesus' base in this chapter, was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee; the foundations of its synagogue and a house venerated as Peter's can still be seen.
Mark 2: Houses in Galilee had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. Digging through one, as the friends of the paralysed man did, was messy but quite possible. Tax collectors like Levi bought the right to collect tolls and were seen as collaborators.
Mark 3: The Herodians were supporters of the family of Herod the Great, who ruled under Rome. Seeing them plot with Pharisees, who usually resented Herodian rule, shows how unusual the alliance against Jesus was.
Mark 4: Farmers in Galilee often sowed seed by hand and ploughed afterwards, which explains seed landing on paths and rocky ground. The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 metres below sea level, ringed by hills, and sudden violent winds still sweep down onto it.
Mark 5: The Decapolis ('ten cities') east of the lake was a largely Gentile region, which is why there was a large herd of pigs there. In 1986 a fishing boat from the first century was found in the mud of the Sea of Galilee; it would have held about a dozen people.
Mark 6: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee as tetrarch. The Jewish historian Josephus also records that Antipas imprisoned and executed John the Baptist, at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea.
Mark 7: The ritual washing the Pharisees expected was not about hygiene but about ritual purity, part of the 'tradition of the elders' later written down in the Mishnah. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Phoenician port cities on the coast of what is now Lebanon.
Mark 8: Caesarea Philippi stood at the springs of Mount Hermon, beside a cave shrine to the Greek god Pan. Philip the tetrarch rebuilt the town and named it for Caesar. Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ was made in this very pagan setting.
Mark 9: Tradition from the fourth century places the transfiguration on Mount Tabor in Galilee, though many scholars suggest Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi. Millstones of the kind Jesus mentions were heavy basalt stones turned by a donkey.
Mark 10: Under Jewish law of the time a husband could divorce his wife, but a wife generally could not initiate divorce, so Jesus' words in verse 12 reflect Roman law, which let women divorce too. Jericho, where Bartimaeus sat, was a lush oasis city on the road up to Jerusalem.
Mark 11: Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims at Passover. The money changers swapped Roman and Greek coins for Tyrian shekels, the coin required for the temple tax. They traded in the Court of the Gentiles, the one area where non-Jews could pray.
Mark 12: The coin Jesus asked for was a silver denarius, a day's wage, stamped with the head of the emperor Tiberius. The widow's two small coins were lepta, the smallest bronze coins in circulation.
Mark 13: Herod the Great's rebuilt temple was famous for its huge white stones; some in the surviving retaining walls weigh many tons. Within forty years, in AD 70, Roman legions under Titus destroyed it, as Jesus had foretold.
Mark 14: Gethsemane means 'oil press', and olive groves still grow on the slope of the Mount of Olives. The Passover meal was eaten reclining, with roast lamb, unleavened bread, bitter herbs and cups of wine.
Mark 15: Pontius Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 bears his name and title. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels, designed to be public and shameful.
Mark 16: Wealthy families in Judea cut tombs into rock, sealed with a large stone. Rolling stones were usually disc-shaped and set in a groove. The women came at dawn on Sunday because the Sabbath had prevented them from anointing the body earlier.
James 1: This letter is traditionally credited to James, the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem. Josephus records his death by stoning in AD 62. 'The twelve tribes in the dispersion' means Jewish believers scattered beyond the land of Israel.
James 2: Synagogues had seats of honour near the front facing the congregation. The gold rings James mentions marked the equestrian class, the rich second tier of Roman society.
James 3: Teachers were highly respected in Jewish communities, so James warns that few should seek the role. His images of bits for horses and rudders for ships were familiar to anyone around the Mediterranean.
James 4: Merchants travelled the trade routes for a year at a time, buying and selling across cities. James addresses that confident business planning when he says, 'you are a mist that appears for a little while.'
James 5: Day labourers were paid at sunset, as the law of Moses required (Deuteronomy 24:15). Withholding wages could leave a family without food. The 'early and late rain' fell in October and in March and April in the land of Israel.
Luke 1: Luke was a physician and a travelling companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14). He tells Theophilus he has investigated everything carefully. Zechariah's priestly division was one of 24 that took turns serving at the temple, so being chosen to burn incense was likely a once-in-a-lifetime honour.
Luke 2: Caesar Augustus ruled from 27 BC to AD 14 and ordered several censuses across the empire. The 'manger' was a feeding trough, often cut from stone, in a house where animals were kept on the lower level or in a cave.
Luke 3: Luke dates John's ministry precisely: the fifteenth year of Tiberius, about AD 28 or 29. The rulers he names, Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, are all known from other ancient sources.
Luke 4: Nazareth was a small village of perhaps a few hundred people. In synagogues of the time a reader stood to read from a scroll and then sat down to teach. Jesus read from Isaiah 61.
Luke 5: Fishermen on the Sea of Galilee worked at night with trammel nets and spent the morning cleaning and mending them. A good catch was salted and shipped from Magdala, a town whose name means 'tower', possibly for its fish-drying towers.
Luke 6: Grain fields could be gleaned by hand by travellers, as Deuteronomy 23:25 allowed. The Pharisees' complaint was that plucking and rubbing the heads counted as harvesting and threshing, which was forbidden on the Sabbath.
Luke 7: A centurion commanded about 80 soldiers. This one, likely serving Herod Antipas, had paid to build the synagogue at Capernaum. At formal dinners guests reclined on couches with their feet away from the table, which is how the woman could reach Jesus' feet.
Luke 8: Luke names women who funded Jesus' travels, including Joanna, wife of Chuza, the manager of Herod Antipas's household. This shows his message reached even into Herod's court.
Luke 9: Bethsaida, near where the 5,000 were fed, was a fishing town at the north end of the lake. It was the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip. Samaritan villages often refused Jews travelling to Jerusalem because of a centuries-old dispute over the right place of worship.
Luke 10: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about 1,000 metres in 27 kilometres through rocky desert and was notorious for robbers. Samaritans and Jews had been bitter rivals since the return from exile, which makes the hero of the parable startling.
Luke 11: The 'sign of Jonah' recalls the prophet whose preaching led Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, to repent. Pharisees tithed even garden herbs like mint and rue, going beyond what the law required.
Luke 12: Barns in Galilee were storehouses for grain, oil and wine. A rich farmer could profit by holding grain until prices rose in a lean year. Sparrows were sold in the market as the cheapest food, two for an assarion, a small copper coin.
Luke 13: Pilate's killing of Galileans while they offered sacrifices is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits other clashes Josephus describes. The tower in Siloam probably stood near the Pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem.
Luke 14: Seating at banquets showed rank, and hosts sent a second summons when the meal was ready. Refusing it at the last moment was a public insult. Rich hosts often invited guests who could repay them, which is the custom Jesus overturns.
Luke 15: Shepherds counted their flocks as they entered the fold at night. The ten silver coins may have been a woman's dowry, sometimes worn on a headdress. A son asking for his inheritance early was in effect wishing his father dead.
Luke 16: Estate managers in the ancient world ran their masters' business and often added their own commission to debts. Reducing the bills may have meant cutting out his own share. Purple cloth, dyed with a costly extract of murex shells, was a sign of great wealth.
Luke 17: Lepers had to live apart from towns and call out a warning when people approached (Leviticus 13:45-46). A healed leper had to be inspected by a priest before rejoining society, which is why Jesus sent the ten to the priests.
Luke 18: Widows had few legal protections and often depended on judges for justice. The Pharisee in the parable fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays, a pious custom of the time that went beyond the law.
Luke 19: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector at Jericho, a customs post on the trade route between Judea and Perea. The parable of the minas echoes real events: Archelaus, son of Herod, went to Rome to receive his kingdom in 4 BC and a Jewish delegation followed to oppose him.
Luke 20: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple. They accepted only the five books of Moses as binding and denied the resurrection, which is why they posed their question about a woman with seven husbands.
Luke 21: Temple offerings went into trumpet-shaped chests in the Court of the Women. Luke records the warning that Jerusalem would be 'surrounded by armies'. When the Romans besieged the city, Christians, according to the historian Eusebius, fled to Pella across the Jordan.
Luke 22: Thirty pieces of silver, in Matthew's account, was the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32. The Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, met at dawn because a formal verdict could not be given at night.
Luke 23: Only Luke records that Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, who was in Jerusalem for Passover. Executions took place outside the city walls by a road so passers-by would see. The site of Golgotha is traditionally placed under the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Luke 24: Emmaus was a village about 11 kilometres (60 stadia) from Jerusalem. The disciples recognized Jesus as he broke bread, the same action he had used at the feeding of the 5,000 and the Last Supper.
Acts 1: Acts is the second volume of Luke's work, also addressed to Theophilus. The upper room may have been in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12). The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.
Acts 2: Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks, came fifty days after Passover and drew Jewish pilgrims from across the empire. The list of nations in verses 9 to 11 stretches from Persia in the east to Rome in the west.
Acts 3: The Beautiful Gate was probably the bronze Nicanor Gate, which Josephus says was more richly decorated than gates plated with silver and gold. Solomon's Portico was a long covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts.
Acts 4: The captain of the temple guard was second in rank to the high priest. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, and five of his sons later held the office, so his family dominated the priesthood for decades.
Acts 5: Gamaliel was one of the most respected teachers of his day, the grandson of the famous Rabbi Hillel. The rebels he mentions, Theudas and Judas the Galilean, both led uprisings that Rome crushed. Judas's revolt was over the census of AD 6.
Acts 6: The 'Hellenists' were Greek-speaking Jews from the wider empire who had settled in Jerusalem, while the 'Hebrews' spoke Aramaic. The seven men chosen all have Greek names. The Synagogue of the Freedmen was formed by descendants of Jews once enslaved by Rome.
Acts 7: Stephen's speech retells Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon. Stoning was carried out outside the city walls. The witnesses laid their cloaks at Saul's feet, which marks him as a man of standing who approved the execution.
Acts 8: Samaria was the region between Judea and Galilee. Ethiopia in the ancient sense meant the Kingdom of Kush, in what is now Sudan. 'Candace' was a title for its queens, who ruled from Meroë.
Acts 9: Damascus had a large Jewish community with several synagogues. Straight Street still runs east to west through the old city. Joppa, the modern Jaffa, was the port where Jonah once boarded a ship to flee from God.
Acts 10: Caesarea Maritima was the Roman capital of Judea, a harbour city built by Herod the Great with a theatre, hippodrome and temple to Augustus. Cornelius belonged to the Italian Cohort, a unit of Roman soldiers recruited in Italy.
Acts 11: Antioch in Syria was the third-largest city in the empire, after Rome and Alexandria. Believers there were first called 'Christians'. The famine foretold by Agabus came during the reign of Claudius (AD 41-54), who faced several food shortages.
Acts 12: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44. Josephus gives a parallel account of his sudden death at Caesarea after he was hailed as a god while dressed in a robe of silver.
Acts 13: Cyprus was Barnabas's home island. Its governor, Sergius Paulus, may be the same man named in an inscription from Rome as one of the city's river commissioners. Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony in the hills of what is now central Turkey.
Acts 14: Lystra had a local legend that Zeus and Hermes had once visited the region in human form, which explains why the crowd took Barnabas for Zeus and Paul, the speaker, for Hermes. Inscriptions linking the two gods have been found nearby.
Acts 15: The Jerusalem council met around AD 49 to decide whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The four requests in the letter helped Jewish and Gentile believers share meals together.
Acts 16: Philippi was a Roman colony settled by veterans of the battle fought there in 42 BC, when Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius. Lydia sold purple cloth from Thyatira, a city known for its dyers' guild.
Acts 17: The Areopagus, 'the hill of Ares', was both a rocky hill below the Acropolis and the name of Athens' ancient council. Paul quotes Greek poets, including Aratus: 'for we are indeed his offspring.'
Acts 18: An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term as governor of Achaia to about AD 51 or 52, one of the firmest dates in Paul's life. Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome around AD 49, which is why Priscilla and Aquila were in Corinth.
Acts 19: Ephesus was home to the temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Its great theatre, where the riot happened, held about 25,000 people and still stands today.
Acts 20: Troas was a port near the site of ancient Troy. Third-storey rooms in crowded tenements were hot, especially with oil lamps burning, which may explain why Eutychus fell asleep. Miletus was a harbour city south of Ephesus.
Acts 21: Warning notices in Greek and Latin forbade Gentiles from passing beyond a barrier in the temple on pain of death. Two of these inscriptions have been found. The Roman garrison was quartered in the Antonia Fortress, overlooking the temple courts.
Acts 22: Paul was born in Tarsus in Cilicia, a centre of learning. Roman citizens could not be flogged or bound without trial. Claiming citizenship falsely was a capital crime, so a claim was usually believed.
Acts 23: Felix governed Judea from about AD 52 to 59. The Roman historian Tacitus said he 'exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave'. Paul was taken under heavy guard to Caesarea, about 100 kilometres away.
Acts 24: Drusilla, Felix's wife, was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Felix kept Paul in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe, until he was replaced by Porcius Festus.
Acts 25: Any Roman citizen could appeal to Caesar, moving the case to the emperor's court in Rome. In AD 59 the emperor was Nero, though his early reign was still regarded as fair.
Acts 26: Herod Agrippa II, the last of the Herodian kings, ruled territories north and east of Galilee. Bernice was his sister. Agrippa was considered an expert in Jewish customs, which is why Festus wanted his advice.
Acts 27: Sailing in the Mediterranean was dangerous after the Day of Atonement in late September or October, and shipping mostly stopped from November to March. Alexandrian grain ships carried Egypt's wheat to feed Rome and could hold hundreds of passengers.
Acts 28: Malta lies south of Sicily. Paul then sailed to Puteoli near Naples and walked to Rome along the Appian Way. The Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns were rest stops on that road, 43 and 33 Roman miles from the city.
Galatians 1: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor, named for Celtic tribes who settled there in the third century BC. Paul probably wrote to the churches he founded on his first journey: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.
Galatians 2: Antioch's church was mixed Jewish and Gentile. Jewish food laws made shared meals a sensitive matter, which is why Peter's withdrawal from eating with Gentiles was so serious to Paul.
Galatians 3: Once a will or covenant had been ratified, no one else could cancel it or add conditions to it. Paul uses that everyday rule to show that the promise to Abraham, given 430 years before the law at Sinai, still stands.
Galatians 4: Wealthy Roman families put children under the care of guardians and stewards until a set age, when the father declared them heirs. Paul says believers have now reached that 'fullness of time'.
Galatians 5: Lists of virtues and vices were common in Greek moral writing. Paul's 'fruit of the Spirit' borrows the form but places the source of goodness in God's Spirit rather than self-discipline.
Galatians 6: Letters were usually dictated to a scribe. Paul adds a closing in his own handwriting, with 'large letters', a personal seal on the letter's authority, much like a signature.
1 Thessalonians 1: Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia, sat on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road linking Rome to the East. The city still exists as Thessaloniki. This letter, from about AD 50 or 51, may be Paul's earliest surviving letter.
1 Thessalonians 2: Wandering philosophers often preached for money and flattered their audiences. Paul points out that he worked with his hands, probably as a tentmaker or leatherworker, so he would not be a burden.
1 Thessalonians 3: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica after only a few weeks (Acts 17). He sent Timothy back from Athens to check on the new believers, and this letter was written in relief at Timothy's good report.
1 Thessalonians 4: The word for the Lord's 'coming' (parousia) was also used for the formal arrival of an emperor or governor visiting a city, when its citizens went out to meet him and escort him in.
1 Thessalonians 5: 'Peace and security' was a slogan of Roman propaganda celebrating the Pax Romana. Paul warns that such human security is not lasting.
2 Thessalonians 1: Written soon after the first letter, this one encourages a church facing ongoing persecution. Thessalonica was a 'free city' with its own magistrates, called politarchs, a title confirmed by inscriptions found there.
2 Thessalonians 2: Some in the church had been unsettled by a report, perhaps a forged letter, that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul reminds them of teaching he had given in person.
2 Thessalonians 3: Greek cities had a culture of patrons supporting clients who did no work. Paul's command that 'if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat' urges believers not to depend on others when they can provide for themselves.
1 Corinthians 1: Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC after being destroyed in 146 BC. It controlled the isthmus between two seas and became a rich, diverse trading city. Paul wrote from Ephesus around AD 53 to 55.
1 Corinthians 2: Greek audiences prized rhetoric, the art of persuasive speaking, and paid well for skilled orators. Paul says he deliberately avoided 'lofty speech or wisdom' when he first came to Corinth.
1 Corinthians 3: Builders in Corinth worked with stone, timber and thatch. Fires were common, and only stone and precious materials survived them, which gives force to Paul's image of work tested by fire.
1 Corinthians 4: Victorious Roman generals paraded captives through the streets, and the condemned were put on show last in the arena. Paul compares the apostles to those 'sentenced to death' in the procession.
1 Corinthians 5: Passover required removing all leaven from the house. Paul may have written near the spring feast, since he speaks of Christ as 'our Passover lamb' and of clearing out the old leaven.
1 Corinthians 6: Roman courts favoured the wealthy, and lawsuits were a way to shame rivals. Paul is troubled that believers were taking one another before pagan magistrates.
1 Corinthians 7: Paul refers to 'the present distress'. Famines struck the region around AD 51, as inscriptions honouring a grain official at Corinth suggest, and this may have shaped his advice on marriage.
1 Corinthians 8: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been sacrificed in a temple, and temple dining rooms were used for banquets. Several such dining rooms have been excavated at the shrine of Asclepius in Corinth.
1 Corinthians 9: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Winners received a crown of pine or wilted celery, which is the 'perishable wreath' Paul contrasts with an imperishable one.
1 Corinthians 10: Paul retells Israel's journey through the wilderness: the cloud, the sea, the manna and the water from the rock. He applies it to a church surrounded by temples and pagan feasts.
1 Corinthians 11: Church gatherings met in the homes of wealthier members. Villas had a dining room that held perhaps nine to twelve reclining guests, with others in the courtyard. This may explain why some ate well while others went hungry.
1 Corinthians 12: The image of the body was used by Roman writers such as Livy to tell lower classes to stay in their place. Paul uses it the other way round, giving special honour to the parts that seem weaker.
1 Corinthians 13: Corinth was famous for bronze, and its mirrors were made of polished metal, which gave only a dim reflection. That is why Paul says 'now we see in a mirror dimly.'
1 Corinthians 14: Greek religion had ecstatic cults, such as the oracle at Delphi, where frenzied speech was prized. Paul insists Christian worship should be orderly and understandable to visitors.
1 Corinthians 15: Verses 3 to 7 contain what many historians regard as a very early Christian creed. Paul received it within a few years of the resurrection, and it names witnesses, many of whom were still alive when he wrote.
1 Corinthians 16: Paul was collecting money from Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He planned to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, when the sailing season was open.
2 Corinthians 1: Paul wrote from Macedonia about a year after 1 Corinthians. He speaks of an affliction in Asia so severe that he despaired of life, perhaps linked to the riot in Ephesus.
2 Corinthians 2: A Roman triumph led captives through the city while incense burned along the route. To the victors the scent meant life and celebration, and to the prisoners it meant death.
2 Corinthians 3: Travelling teachers carried letters of recommendation from patrons or churches. Paul says the Corinthian believers are his letter, 'written on our hearts.'
2 Corinthians 4: Small clay oil lamps were the cheapest household items, used and thrown away. People sometimes hid valuables in clay jars. Paul calls himself such a jar holding a great treasure.
2 Corinthians 5: Paul, a tentmaker, compares the body to a tent. Ambassadors in the Roman world spoke with the full authority of the emperor who sent them.
2 Corinthians 6: 'Unequally yoked' comes from the law against ploughing with an ox and a donkey together (Deuteronomy 22:10). Paul applies it to partnerships with idol worship.
2 Corinthians 7: Titus had carried a painful letter from Paul to Corinth. Paul waited anxiously at Troas and then in Macedonia, and was overjoyed when Titus arrived with good news.
2 Corinthians 8: The Macedonian churches, Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, were poorer than Corinth, yet they gave generously to the Jerusalem collection. Paul arranged for trusted men to carry the money to avoid any suspicion.
2 Corinthians 9: Sowing and harvest language would have been familiar from the farmland around Corinth. Paul quotes Psalm 112 about the generous person whose righteousness endures forever.
2 Corinthians 10: Paul's critics said he was impressive in letters but weak in person. Greek culture valued speakers with commanding presence, and the 'super-apostles' seem to have traded on that.
2 Corinthians 11: Synagogues could punish members with 'forty lashes less one', since Deuteronomy 25:3 limited the number to forty. Paul's escape from Damascus in a basket happened when Aretas IV, king of the Nabateans, controlled the city.
2 Corinthians 12: Paul's 'thorn in the flesh' has been explained many ways, from eye trouble to chronic illness. The 'third heaven' was a Jewish way of speaking of the highest heaven, where God dwells.
2 Corinthians 13: Paul was preparing for a third visit to Corinth. The law required 'two or three witnesses' for any charge (Deuteronomy 19:15), and he applies that rule to his visits.
Romans 1: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem. He had never visited Rome, a city of perhaps a million people, where a church already met in several households.
Romans 2: After Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome around AD 49, the church there was led mainly by Gentiles. When Jewish believers returned under Nero, tensions between the two groups may lie behind this chapter.
Romans 3: The 'propitiation' or 'mercy seat' was the gold cover of the ark of the covenant. The high priest sprinkled blood on it on the Day of Atonement. Paul uses the word for Christ's death.
Romans 4: Abraham was honoured by Jews as the father of the nation. Paul notes that God counted Abraham righteous in Genesis 15, years before his circumcision in Genesis 17.
Romans 5: Paul contrasts Adam and Christ as heads of two humanities. Rome itself was used to the idea of one man's actions shaping the destiny of a whole people, from Romulus to Augustus.
Romans 6: Slavery was everywhere in Rome; perhaps a third of the city's people were enslaved. Paul's language of being 'slaves of righteousness' would have struck readers vividly.
Romans 7: Roman law said a married woman was bound to her husband while he lived. Paul's example in verses 1 to 3 would have been clear to readers in the capital.
Romans 8: Roman adoption gave the adopted son full legal rights as heir, wiping away old debts. Emperors such as Augustus and Tiberius became heirs through adoption.
Romans 9: Paul quotes Hosea, Isaiah, Exodus and Genesis in quick succession. Jewish teachers often strung texts together this way to build an argument.
Romans 10: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30 and Joel 2. Roman roads and peaceful sea routes let messengers carry news across the empire faster than ever before, a fact Paul celebrates in verses 14 and 15.
Romans 11: Olive growers grafted shoots from cultivated trees onto wild stock. Paul's image of wild branches grafted into a cultivated tree reverses normal practice, to show that the Gentiles' inclusion is God's grace.
Romans 12: Sacrifices in Rome's many temples involved animals. Paul speaks instead of 'a living sacrifice', the whole person offered to God.
Romans 13: Nero's early reign was considered a good period. In AD 58 there was public protest in Rome over taxes, recorded by Tacitus, which gives background to Paul's instruction to pay what is due.
Romans 14: Rome's markets sold meat that had been offered to idols, and some Jewish believers kept to vegetables to avoid it. Others kept the Sabbath and feast days. Paul asks both groups to welcome each other.
Romans 15: Paul hoped to visit Rome on his way to Spain, the western edge of the known world. Early writers such as Clement of Rome suggest he may have reached 'the limits of the West'.
Romans 16: Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, probably carried the letter to Rome. Erastus, the city treasurer, may be the Erastus named in a Corinthian paving inscription as an official who paid for the pavement.
John 1: Tradition says John wrote this Gospel in Ephesus late in the first century. 'The Word' (Logos) was a term both Greek philosophers and Jewish writers such as Philo used. John begins his Gospel with the same words as Genesis: 'In the beginning'.
John 2: Cana was a village in Galilee. A wedding feast could last a week, and running out of wine would shame the family. Each stone water jar held 20 to 30 gallons; stone was used because it could not become ritually unclean.
John 3: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin. Coming at night may have been for privacy, or simply because evening was a common time for teachers to talk.
John 4: Jacob's well near Sychar is still visited today and is about 40 metres deep. The Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, where their temple had stood until a Jewish ruler destroyed it in about 110 BC.
John 5: The Pool of Bethesda was excavated near St Anne's Church in Jerusalem. It had five porticoes, as John describes, around two large basins.
John 6: Barley loaves were the bread of the poor. Manna in the wilderness was a symbol of God's provision, and many expected the Messiah to bring it back.
John 7: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was an autumn harvest festival. Each day, priests carried water from the Pool of Siloam to pour at the altar, which gives force to Jesus' cry, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.'
John 8: During the Feast of Booths, huge golden lamps were lit in the Court of the Women and lit up all Jerusalem. Jesus' words 'I am the light of the world' were spoken in that setting.
John 9: The Pool of Siloam was rediscovered in 2004, with wide steps leading down to the water. It was fed by Hezekiah's tunnel, cut through rock around 700 BC.
John 10: The Feast of Dedication, now called Hanukkah, celebrates the Maccabees cleansing the temple in 164 BC after it was defiled by the Greek king Antiochus IV. Shepherds' sheepfolds were stone enclosures, and the shepherd sometimes slept across the gap.
John 11: Bethany was a village about three kilometres from Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives. Jewish custom held mourning for seven days, and professional mourners were often hired.
John 12: Pure nard was a perfume imported from the Himalayas. Mary's pound of it was worth about 300 denarii, close to a year's wages for a labourer.
John 13: Washing feet was the job of the lowest servant, and some Jewish teachers said it should not even be asked of Jewish slaves. Guests reclined on couches around a low table, which explains how the beloved disciple leaned against Jesus.
John 14: A wealthy Jewish family's house was often built with rooms around a courtyard, added on as sons married. Jesus' 'my Father's house has many rooms' draws on that picture.
John 15: Vines grew on the terraced hillsides of Judea, and a golden vine decorated the entrance to the temple sanctuary. Vinedressers pruned hard in the winter and spring.
John 16: 'Put out of the synagogue' meant losing community, family ties and work. By the end of the first century, believers in Jesus faced this in many places.
John 17: This prayer is often called Jesus' 'high priestly prayer', since he intercedes for his followers as the high priest did for Israel.
John 18: The Kidron Valley runs between the city and the Mount of Olives. Caiaphas was high priest from AD 18 to 36. An ossuary (bone box) bearing the name 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' was found in Jerusalem in 1990.
John 19: The Gabbatha pavement may have been at Herod's palace, where Roman governors stayed in Jerusalem. The sign on the cross was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, the languages of the people, the government and trade.
John 20: In the ancient world, women's testimony was often given little weight in court. That the first witnesses to the empty tomb were women is seen by many historians as a mark of the account's authenticity.
John 21: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its shore. Fishermen worked naked or lightly dressed. The charcoal fire echoes the fire where Peter denied Jesus.
Ephesians 1: Ephesus was the capital of the province of Asia, with a population of perhaps 250,000. Paul spent about three years there. Some early manuscripts lack the words 'in Ephesus', so the letter may have been circulated among several churches.
Ephesians 2: The 'dividing wall of hostility' recalls the barrier in the temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, with warning signs threatening death. Paul says Christ has broken it down.
Ephesians 3: Paul wrote this letter as a prisoner, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62. His house arrest let him receive visitors and write letters.
Ephesians 4: Ephesus was a centre of magic and the occult (Acts 19:19). Paul's call to put off the old self and put on the new uses the image of changing clothes, as at a baptism.
Ephesians 5: Drinking parties in honour of Dionysus, god of wine, were common in Greek cities. Paul contrasts being drunk with wine with being filled with the Spirit and singing psalms and hymns.
Ephesians 6: Paul was chained to a Roman soldier while under house arrest, and the soldier's armour gave him the image of the 'whole armour of God'. Roman legionaries wore a belt, breastplate, hobnailed sandals, a large shield and a helmet.
Philippians 1: Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud of their Roman rights. The 'imperial guard' (praetorium) mentioned in verse 13 were soldiers who guarded Paul while he was a prisoner.
Philippians 2: Verses 6 to 11 are often thought to be an early Christian hymn. Its pattern of humility followed by exaltation stood in contrast to Roman values of honour and status-seeking.
Philippians 3: Paul lists his credentials as a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin and a Pharisee. Citizens of Philippi were registered as citizens of Rome; Paul says believers' citizenship is in heaven.
Philippians 4: Epaphroditus had brought a gift of money from Philippi to Paul in prison. Prisoners in the Roman world depended on friends for food and supplies. 'Those of Caesar's household' were slaves and freedmen in imperial service.
Colossians 1: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in what is now Turkey, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not visited it; the church was founded by Epaphras, one of his co-workers.
Colossians 2: A 'certificate of debt' was a handwritten IOU. When a debt was paid, the document could be cancelled by crossing it out. Paul says God nailed ours to the cross.
Colossians 3: Greek and Roman households had codes setting out duties for husbands, wives, children and slaves. Paul's version addresses each group directly, which was unusual, and places masters under a Master in heaven.
Colossians 4: Laodicea, only about 16 kilometres from Colossae, was a wealthy banking city. An earthquake struck the Lycus valley around AD 60 or 61, according to Tacitus, though Laodicea rebuilt without Roman help.
Philemon 1: Onesimus was a slave who had left his master Philemon in Colossae and met Paul, probably in Rome. Roman law treated a runaway slave harshly. Paul sends him back with this personal letter asking Philemon to receive him as a brother. His name means 'useful'.
Matthew 1: Matthew, a former tax collector, wrote with a Jewish audience in mind. Genealogies were important for proving family rights. Matthew arranges Jesus' ancestors in three groups of fourteen, perhaps because the Hebrew letters of David's name add up to fourteen.
Matthew 2: Herod the Great was a brilliant builder and a ruthless ruler who killed his own wife and three sons. The magi were probably astrologer-priests from Persia or Babylon. Herod died in 4 BC, so Jesus' birth was a little before that.
Matthew 3: The Jordan River flows from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. The traditional baptism site is near Jericho. The Pharisees and Sadducees were rival groups, so it was unusual to see them come together.
Matthew 4: The wilderness of Judea is a dry, rocky region between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. The 'pinnacle of the temple' was probably the southeast corner of the temple platform, which stood high above the Kidron Valley.
Matthew 5: The traditional site of the Sermon on the Mount is a hillside above the Sea of Galilee near Capernaum. A natural slope there carries the voice well. A Roman soldier could legally make a civilian carry his pack one mile.
Matthew 6: Hypocrites, from a Greek word for 'actors', were people who performed for an audience. Moths and rust were real threats to wealth, which was often stored as fine clothes and metal.
Matthew 7: A 'narrow gate' was a small door in a city's main gate, used after the large gates were closed. Houses in Galilee were built on bedrock where possible, because winter rains could turn dry riverbeds into torrents.
Matthew 8: Gadara and Gerasa were Gentile cities of the Decapolis on the east side of the lake. Tombs cut into hillsides were sometimes used as shelters by outcasts.
Matthew 9: Matthew's tax booth was probably on the trade route through Capernaum, collecting tolls for Herod Antipas. Mourners at a funeral included hired flute players and wailing women.
Matthew 10: Travelling teachers often carried a staff and a bag for begging. Jesus told the twelve to travel light and depend on hospitality, which was a strong custom in the Middle East.
Matthew 11: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were the towns where Jesus did most of his miracles. Chorazin's ruins include a synagogue of black basalt, with a carved stone 'seat of Moses'.
Matthew 12: The Pharisees counted 39 types of work forbidden on the Sabbath. Healing that was not a matter of life and death was debated. Jesus pointed to the priests who worked in the temple every Sabbath.
Matthew 13: Mustard plants by the Sea of Galilee can grow to three metres. Leaven was a small lump of old dough kept back to raise the next batch. Treasure was often buried for safekeeping in times of war.
Matthew 14: Herod Antipas held a birthday banquet for officials and military commanders. Salome, Herodias' daughter, later married her uncle Philip the tetrarch. The 'fourth watch of the night' was 3 to 6 in the morning.
Matthew 15: Canaanites were the ancient inhabitants of the land before Israel. Matthew uses the old name for this Gentile woman from the region of Tyre and Sidon, which makes her faith all the more striking.
Matthew 16: The Sadducees' signs request came from a group that did not believe in angels or resurrection. Peter's name means 'rock' in Greek (Petros), as Cephas does in Aramaic.
Matthew 17: The temple tax was half a shekel, paid each year by every Jewish man. A shekel coin found in a fish's mouth would pay for two people. Tilapia, now called 'St Peter's fish', are common in the lake.
Matthew 18: A talent was about 6,000 denarii, roughly 20 years' wages for a labourer. Ten thousand talents was more than the yearly tax income of all of Herod's kingdom, an impossible debt.
Matthew 19: Two leading rabbis of the time disagreed over divorce: Shammai allowed it only for sexual immorality, while Hillel allowed it for almost any reason. The Pharisees were asking Jesus to take a side.
Matthew 20: Day labourers waited in the marketplace to be hired, and the working day ran from sunrise to sunset. A denarius was a standard day's wage for this kind of work.
Matthew 21: Zechariah 9:9 foretold a king riding on a donkey. Kings rode war horses into battle and donkeys in peace. The crowds cried 'Hosanna', meaning 'save us', from Psalm 118.
Matthew 22: Wedding feasts were invitation-only events, and a host might provide clothing for guests. Coming without proper dress dishonoured the host.
Matthew 23: Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing scripture verses, worn on the forehead and arm during prayer. Tombs were whitewashed before Passover so pilgrims would not touch them and become unclean.
Matthew 24: Josephus describes the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 in great detail: famine, false prophets and the burning of the temple. Many believers fled the city before the siege closed in.
Matthew 25: Weddings were held in the evening, and the bridegroom came to fetch his bride, accompanied by a torch-lit procession. A talent was a huge sum, so even the servant given one talent had been trusted with a fortune.
Matthew 26: The Passover lamb was killed at the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan. Thirty pieces of silver recalls Zechariah 11:12, where it was the wage paid to a rejected shepherd.
Matthew 27: Pilate's wife sent a warning about her dream; Romans took dreams seriously as omens. The 'potter's field' was later called Akeldama, the 'field of blood', and is traditionally located in the Hinnom Valley.
Matthew 28: Matthew records that the chief priests paid the guards to say the disciples stole the body, and that this story was still told 'to this day'. Galilee, where Jesus met the eleven, was where his ministry began.
1 Timothy 1: Timothy was Paul's young co-worker from Lystra, with a Greek father and a Jewish mother. Paul left him in Ephesus to lead the church. This is one of the three 'pastoral letters' written to church leaders.
1 Timothy 2: The temple of Artemis in Ephesus had a large staff of priestesses. Paul's instructions about worship were written to a church in a city shaped by that cult.
1 Timothy 3: Overseers (bishops) and deacons led house churches. The qualities Paul lists, like being hospitable and managing one's household well, mattered because churches met in members' homes.
1 Timothy 4: Some teachers in Ephesus were forbidding marriage and certain foods, ideas linked to early forms of Gnostic thought that treated the physical world as evil. Paul answers that everything God created is good.
1 Timothy 5: Rome had no public welfare system, and widows without family were often destitute. The early church kept a list of widows it supported, an arrangement that impressed even pagan observers.
1 Timothy 6: Ephesus was a wealthy commercial city. Paul's words 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' echo a saying also found in Greek moral writers.
2 Timothy 1: This is probably Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome around AD 64 to 67, during Nero's persecution. Tradition says Paul was beheaded on the road to Ostia, outside Rome.
2 Timothy 2: Paul uses three images: a soldier, an athlete and a farmer. Each was a familiar figure in the Roman world. Soldiers served at least 20 years and could not take on civilian business.
2 Timothy 3: Jannes and Moses' other opponent, Jambres, are not named in Exodus. Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh's magicians.
2 Timothy 4: Roman prisons were cold, dark and damp. Paul asks for his cloak before winter, and for his scrolls and parchments. Only Luke is with him.
Titus 1: Titus was a Greek co-worker of Paul's. Paul quotes the Cretan poet Epimenides, who wrote around 600 BC that 'Cretans are always liars'. The island was known for its rough reputation.
Titus 2: Household codes were common in Greek moral writing. Paul gives instructions to older and younger men and women and to slaves, so the gospel would be 'adorned' in the eyes of outsiders.
Titus 3: Crete was under Roman rule. Paul urges respect for rulers and authorities. Nicopolis, where he planned to spend the winter, was a city on the west coast of Greece founded by Augustus.
Hebrews 1: The author of Hebrews is not named; early suggestions included Paul, Barnabas and Apollos. The letter was probably written before AD 70, since it speaks of temple sacrifices as still going on.
Hebrews 2: Angels were thought to have delivered the law at Sinai, a Jewish tradition reflected in Acts 7:53. The writer argues that the Son is greater than the angels.
Hebrews 3: Moses was revered as the greatest prophet and lawgiver. The writer quotes Psalm 95, which recalls Israel's rebellion at Meribah in the wilderness.
Hebrews 4: The Sabbath rest pointed back to God resting after creation. Joshua's name in Greek is Iēsous, the same as Jesus, which adds weight to the comparison in verse 8.
Hebrews 5: Melchizedek was a priest-king of Salem in Genesis 14 who blessed Abraham. Psalm 110 speaks of a priest 'after the order of Melchizedek', a passage the writer applies to Christ.
Hebrews 6: An anchor was a common symbol of hope in the ancient world, and it appears carved on many early Christian tombs in the catacombs of Rome.
Hebrews 7: Priests in Israel came from the tribe of Levi. Jesus was from the tribe of Judah, so the writer points to Melchizedek's priesthood, which came before Levi's.
Hebrews 8: The writer quotes Jeremiah 31, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, about a new covenant written on the heart.
Hebrews 9: The tabernacle had two rooms: the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, entered only once a year by the high priest on the Day of Atonement. The ark of the covenant held the tablets, Aaron's staff and a jar of manna.
Hebrews 10: Animal sacrifices were offered daily at the temple. The writer quotes Psalm 40, 'sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me.'
Hebrews 11: The heroes of faith listed here run from Abel to the prophets. 'Sawn in two' may refer to a Jewish tradition that Isaiah was martyred this way under King Manasseh.
Hebrews 12: Greek stadiums had seats around the track for spectators. The 'great cloud of witnesses' pictures the heroes of chapter 11 cheering on runners in the race.
Hebrews 13: Sacrificed animals on the Day of Atonement were burned outside the camp. Jesus also suffered outside the city gate. Christians who were imprisoned depended on fellow believers for food and support.
1 Peter 1: Peter wrote to believers in five Roman provinces in what is now Turkey. 'Babylon', where he says he is writing from, was probably a code name for Rome. He calls his readers 'exiles', strangers in their own society.
1 Peter 2: Gentile believers who stopped attending temple feasts and civic festivals were accused of being anti-social. Peter urges them to live so well that their neighbours would have no grounds for slander.
1 Peter 3: Wealthy Roman women wore elaborate braided hairstyles and gold jewellery as signs of status. Portrait busts from the period show these styles in detail.
1 Peter 4: In AD 64 a great fire burned much of Rome. Nero blamed the Christians, and Tacitus describes believers being burned as torches in his gardens. Peter may be writing as this 'fiery trial' began.
1 Peter 5: Silvanus (Silas), Paul's former companion, helped write the letter. Mark, whom Peter calls 'my son', is linked with Peter in Rome by early tradition. Lions were used in the arena to kill condemned prisoners.
2 Peter 1: Peter writes knowing his death is near, as Jesus had foretold (John 21:18-19). Tradition says he was crucified in Rome under Nero, upside down at his own request. He recalls witnessing the transfiguration.
2 Peter 2: Some false teachers claimed freedom from moral rules. Peter recalls God's judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah, cities whose destruction near the Dead Sea was remembered as a warning.
2 Peter 3: Some mockers said nothing had changed since the world began. Peter answers that God measures time differently, quoting Psalm 90: 'a thousand years are as one day.' He calls Paul's letters 'Scripture', showing they were already being collected.
Jude 1: Jude was a brother of Jesus and James. He quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing popular at the time, and refers to a dispute over the body of Moses found in Jewish tradition.
1 John 1: Tradition says the apostle John lived to old age in Ephesus. He writes to churches troubled by teachers who denied that Jesus came in the flesh. He opens with what he had heard, seen and touched.
1 John 2: John's 'little children' suggests an elderly leader speaking with affection. Some members had left the church to follow the false teachers.
1 John 3: Cain killing Abel was a familiar example in Jewish teaching of jealousy and hatred. John uses it to contrast hatred with love.
1 John 4: Early Gnostic teachers such as Cerinthus, who lived in Ephesus, taught that the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the crucifixion. John insists Jesus Christ came in the flesh.
1 John 5: 'Water and blood' may refer to Jesus' baptism and his death. John wrote to give believers assurance, so that 'you may know that you have eternal life.'
2 John 1: This is one of the shortest books in the Bible, short enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. Travelling teachers depended on hospitality, so John warns not to host those who deny Christ came in the flesh.
3 John 1: Gaius was a generous host for travelling missionaries. Diotrephes, a local leader, refused to welcome them. The letter shows how much the early mission relied on believers opening their homes.
Revelation 1: John received the vision on Patmos, a small rocky island off the coast of Asia Minor, where he had been exiled. Early writers date the book to the reign of Domitian (AD 81-96), who demanded to be honoured as 'lord and god'.
Revelation 2: The seven churches lay on a circular road through the province of Asia, in the order a messenger would visit them. Ephesus' harbour was silting up. Smyrna was famed for loyalty to Rome. Pergamum had a great altar to Zeus. Thyatira had many trade guilds.
Revelation 3: Sardis had been captured twice by enemies who climbed its cliffs while the guards slept. Laodicea's water came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm, unlike Hierapolis' hot springs or Colossae's cold water. Laodicea was also known for banking and eye salve.
Revelation 4: Roman emperors held court surrounded by attendants, and subject kings laid their crowns before them. The 24 elders casting their crowns before God's throne would have reminded readers of such scenes.
Revelation 5: Scrolls of legal importance, such as wills, were sealed with seven seals by seven witnesses. Only the rightful heir could open them.
Revelation 6: Parthian horsemen, Rome's feared enemies beyond the Euphrates, were famous mounted archers, which gives colour to the rider with a bow. A denarius for a quart of wheat was about eight to ten times the normal price, a sign of famine.
Revelation 7: The number twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Palm branches were waved at the Feast of Booths and at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
Revelation 8: Incense was burned morning and evening on the golden altar in the temple. Trumpets announced festivals, war and the new year in Israel.
Revelation 9: Locust swarms were a familiar disaster in the Middle East, darkening the sky and stripping fields bare. The Euphrates River was the eastern border of the Roman Empire.
Revelation 10: Eating a scroll recalls Ezekiel 3, where the prophet eats a scroll that tastes sweet as honey.
Revelation 11: Measuring the temple recalls Ezekiel 40-42. The two witnesses echo Moses and Elijah, who turned water to blood and shut up the sky.
Revelation 12: Greek and Roman myths told of a dragon threatening a goddess about to give birth. Leto fled from the serpent Python. Revelation uses familiar imagery to tell a deeper story.
Revelation 13: The province of Asia had temples to the emperors in several cities, and local officials promoted emperor worship. Refusing to take part could mean losing work or trade.
Revelation 14: Wine presses were stone basins where grapes were trodden underfoot. Juice ran out through a channel. The image of judgment as a wine press comes from Isaiah 63 and Joel 3.
Revelation 15: The 'song of Moses' was the song Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15). The seven last plagues echo the plagues on Egypt.
Revelation 16: Armageddon means 'the hill of Megiddo', a fortress city that guarded a key pass. Many famous battles were fought in the valley below, including those of Deborah and King Josiah.
Revelation 17: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills. Roman coins showed the goddess Roma seated on the seven hills beside the Tiber.
Revelation 18: The list of cargo in verses 11 to 13 matches the luxury goods imported into Rome: silk from China, ivory from Africa, cinnamon from India and marble from across the empire.
Revelation 19: Roman generals rode white horses in their triumphal parades. The rider of the white horse here wears many crowns, a sign of kingship over many nations.
Revelation 20: The thousand-year reign has been understood in different ways by Christians throughout history. The image of a great white throne draws on Daniel 7.
Revelation 21: The new Jerusalem is shaped like a cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20). Its twelve foundation stones echo the twelve gems on the high priest's breastplate.
Revelation 22: The river of life recalls Ezekiel 47 and the rivers of Eden. The tree of life, lost in Genesis 3, returns, bringing the Bible's story full circle.
